name: Scalp exfoliation
lead: Scalp exfoliation is a hair-care practice that uses physical scrubs, chemical exfoliants such as salicylic or glycolic acid, or hybrids to remove dead skin cells, oil and product buildup from the scalp.[1] People use it to reduce visible flakes, leave hair looking cleaner and fuller at the roots, and keep a clear scalp as a base for hair-care products, which they say supports healthy-looking hair and hair growth.[1][4]

Salicylic acid is an FDA-approved over-the-counter anti-dandruff active, and dandruff shampoos combine actives such as zinc pyrithione and ketoconazole.[2] Wikipedia's article on cosmetic exfoliation describes chemical exfoliants as acids and enzymes that loosen bonds between dead skin cells, with beta-hydroxy acids such as salicylic acid acting within pores, and notes dermatologists say exfoliation is not medically necessary because skin sheds naturally.[5]
One 2024 study evaluated a hydroxy acid scrub combined with a copper tripeptide serum in adults with seborrheic dermatitis.[3] No studies were found testing scalp exfoliation for hair growth.

paras: Physical exfoliants use granules such as sugar, sea salt or charcoal, rubbed in with massage. Chemical exfoliants use acids that dissolve bonds between dead skin cells.[1]

Wikipedia notes that chemical exfoliation is often suggested for acne and that overdoing exfoliation can damage the skin barrier, causing tightness, sensitivity, redness and dryness.[5] On T Nation, a poster advised massaging shampoo in gently with the fingertips instead of rough scrubbing, and another suggested scalp massage may support blood flow.[6] A TRT-focused poster described gently scrubbing the scalp with fingers on days he used ketoconazole, saying he had read that sebum buildup could accelerate hair loss.[7]

Descriptions claim exfoliation unclogs follicles and supports hair growth.[1] Dermatology references on dandruff describe cause as involving sebum, Malassezia yeasts and individual sensitivity, and list antifungal and keratolytic shampoos as treatments.[2]
Descriptions say over-exfoliation may disrupt the scalp barrier, causing dryness, extra oil or discomfort, and suggest people with psoriasis, eczema or open sores consult a dermatologist.[1]

A 2024 study in Cureus assessed the safety, efficacy and tolerability of a regimen combining a hydroxy acid scrub with a copper tripeptide serum for seborrheic dermatitis in adults.[3] No studies were found on exfoliation alone for hair growth or density.

lore.intro: On T Nation, scalp scrubbing comes up in hair-loss and dandruff threads, usually as gentle washing or fingertip scrubbing alongside medicated shampoo.[6][7]

claims.claim: Clearing sebum and dead skin from the scalp protects hair
claims.believers: One poster using topical ketoconazole said he scrubs his scalp so a thick sebum and dead-skin layer does not form, citing something he had read about hair loss.[7]
claims.experts: Dermatology references describe dandruff as involving sebum, Malassezia yeasts and individual sensitivity, and no studies were found testing exfoliation for hair growth.[2]

claims.believers: A poster in a scalp-health thread wrote that men often scrub too hard and advised gentle fingertip massage.[6]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that over-exfoliation can damage the skin barrier, and Grokipedia's description also warns of dryness and extra oil.[1][5]

card.summary: Scrubs and acids to clear scalp flakes and buildup; some flaking data, no hair-growth trials.

quick.overview:
Scalp exfoliation uses scrubs or acids to remove dead skin and buildup. People use it for flaking and hoping for healthier hair.

Salicylic acid is an approved dandruff active, but no trials tested exfoliation for hair growth.
quick.mechanism: Physical granules rub debris off; acids such as salicylic or glycolic acid loosen bonds between dead skin cells.
quick.risks: Descriptions say overdoing it may cause dryness, oiliness or irritation, and that people with psoriasis, eczema or open sores should consult a dermatologist.

chain: Scrub or acid lifts flakes, oil and buildup
Cleaner scalp with fewer visible flakes
Hair looks cleaner and fuller; products sit on a clear scalp
angle.text: People exfoliate the scalp to cut visible flaking and greasy buildup, so hair and parting look cleaner. Proponents also link a clear scalp to healthier-looking growth, which is a claim rather than a tested result.
